topic: GROUP BY and HAVING in SQL

questions.question: What is the GROUP BY clause in SQL and how does it work?
questions.title: GROUP BY Clause in SQL
questions.direct_answer: GROUP BY divides input rows into groups that share the grouping values, then aggregate functions can calculate one result per group. In a standard grouped query, a selected expression must be aggregated, be a grouping expression, or be functionally dependent on the grouping columns where the database supports that rule. Database modes differ, so 'every selected column must appear verbatim in GROUP BY' is a useful beginner rule but not the whole SQL standard.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you understand GROUP BY buckets rows and the SELECT-column rule.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Selecting a non-aggregated column that isn't in GROUP BY.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Explain that GROUP BY runs after WHERE and before HAVING/SELECT.

sections.title: How GROUP BY Forms Summary Rows
sections.content:
GROUP BY does not promise sorted output. Add ORDER BY when display order matters. NULL grouping values normally form one group because grouping treats them as not distinct for this purpose.

Multiple grouping columns create a key tuple. GROUP BY region, status makes one group for each distinct region/status combination. Advanced forms such as ROLLUP and GROUPING SETS add subtotal groups and are database/standard features beyond the basic rule.

sections.title: Quick revision
content: WHERE filters rows before grouping; HAVING filters groups after aggregation.
Each distinct grouping-key combination produces one result group.
Aggregate expressions summarize rows inside that group.
Non-grouped selected columns require a valid functional-dependency rule or an aggregate.

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content:
SELECT department_id, COUNT(*) FROM employee GROUP BY department_id returns one row per department id. Selecting employee_name as well is not meaningful because a group can contain several names. If department_id is a declared key for a joined department table, some standards-compliant databases can infer that department.name is functionally dependent; others require it in GROUP BY. Write portable queries explicitly when multiple engines matter.

For example, SELECT department_id, COUNT(*) FROM employee GROUP BY department_id returns one row per department. A selected non-aggregate column must be grouped or be allowed through a database-supported functional dependency rule.

sections.title: GROUP BY at a Glance
sections.content:
blue|What|~buckets rows|by shared column values|one row per group|enables per-group aggregates
emerald|SELECT rule|~aggregate or grouped|column in GROUP BY|or inside COUNT/SUM|else error
amber|Order|~runs mid-query|after WHERE|before HAVING/SELECT|filter rows first
rose|Multi-column|~finer buckets|GROUP BY a, b|one row per (a,b) pair|order doesn't change result

sections.title: Count per group
sections.content:
```sql
SELECT department, COUNT(*) AS headcount, AVG(salary) AS avg_pay
FROM employees
GROUP BY department;
```

Sample output:

| department | headcount | avg_pay |
|---|---|---|
| Tech | 12 | 95000 |
| Sales | 7 | 60000 |
| Finance | 4 | 88000 |

*One summary row per department.*

sections.title: Wrong: an ungrouped column in SELECT
sections.content:
```sql
-- name is neither aggregated nor in GROUP BY -> error or junk value
SELECT department, name, COUNT(*) AS headcount
FROM employees
GROUP BY department;
```

sections.title: Right: aggregate it or group by it
sections.content:
```sql
-- every selected column is now an aggregate or in GROUP BY
SELECT department, COUNT(*) AS headcount, MAX(name) AS sample_name
FROM employees
GROUP BY department;
```

*Each output row stands for a whole department, so a single row can't show one employee's `name` — wrap it in an aggregate (`MAX`/`MIN`) or add it to `GROUP BY`.*

sections.title: Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Ungrouped column in SELECT**: `SELECT name, department, COUNT(*) GROUP BY department` fails — `name` is neither grouped nor aggregated.
- **Filtering groups in WHERE**: aggregate conditions go in HAVING.
- **Expecting order**: GROUP BY doesn't sort — add ORDER BY if you need it.
- **Grouping by a column you don't need**: extra GROUP BY columns split buckets finer than intended.

speakable_v2.hook: GROUP BY folds rows that share a value into one summary row each. One iron rule decides if your query even runs.
speakable_v2.standard_example: An employees table grouped by department with COUNT and AVG

beats.text: GROUP BY collapses rows that share a value into groups. Then an aggregate like count or sum gives one number per group. So group by department with count gives the headcount for each department.

Without it you only get raw rows. But reports need totals per category. Sales per region, signups per month, headcount per team. GROUP BY turns thousands of rows into a short summary that's easy to read.

items: The grouping columns define each bucket. Group by department makes one bucket per department.
Aggregates summarize each bucket. Count, sum, and avg all work.
The select rule binds it together. Every column must sit in an aggregate or in GROUP BY.

beats.text: Picture an employees table. Group by department, then count star, and you get a headcount per department. Add avg of salary for average pay too. Here's the non-obvious part. The count is per group, not per row, so one line stands for the whole team.

items: Putting an ungrouped column in select. A bare name breaks the query.
Expecting sorted output. GROUP BY doesn't sort, so add ORDER BY yourself.

speakable_v2.cap: So GROUP BY makes one row per bucket, and every plain column has to live in GROUP BY too.

questions.question: What is the HAVING clause in SQL and when do you use it?
questions.title: HAVING Clause in SQL — Filtering Groups
questions.direct_answer: HAVING filters grouped results after grouping and aggregate evaluation in SQL's logical model. It is used for conditions such as COUNT(*) > 5. Row-level conditions normally belong in WHERE because that expresses the intended input set; optimizers may push equivalent predicates, so WHERE is not automatically faster in every physical plan.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you know HAVING filters groups using aggregates after GROUP BY.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Putting aggregate conditions in WHERE, or row conditions in HAVING.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Note WHERE filters before grouping (faster), HAVING after — prefer WHERE when possible.

sections.title: HAVING Filters Groups
sections.content:
Some databases allow HAVING without GROUP BY, treating the entire input as one group or applying vendor extensions. Stick to clear standard forms when portability matters.

Performance comes from the optimized plan. Writing a true row predicate in WHERE often enables early filtering and indexes, but the optimizer can also transform predicates. Verify with EXPLAIN rather than promising a fixed speed difference from clause order alone.

**Example.** SELECT department_id, COUNT(*) AS total FROM employee GROUP BY department_id HAVING COUNT(*) >= 5 keeps only departments with at least five employees. WHERE active=true would first remove inactive employee rows before grouping.

sections.title: Quick revision
content: WHERE decides which rows enter grouping.
HAVING decides which resulting groups remain.
Aggregate conditions generally require HAVING or an outer query.
A predicate on grouping keys can sometimes be placed in either clause with the same result, but WHERE is clearer as a row filter.

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content:
SELECT department_id, COUNT(*) FROM employee WHERE active=true GROUP BY department_id HAVING COUNT(*) > 5 counts active employees and keeps departments with more than five. Moving active=true to HAVING may be invalid or express a different idea depending on selected/grouped expressions. COUNT(*) does not exist for an individual input row, so its predicate belongs after grouping.

For example, WHERE active=true filters employee rows first, while HAVING COUNT(*) >= 5 filters the department groups after COUNT is calculated.

sections.title: HAVING at a Glance
sections.content:
blue|What|~filters groups|after GROUP BY|aggregate conditions OK|COUNT(*) > 5
emerald|vs WHERE|~stage difference|WHERE filters rows first|HAVING filters groups after|both can appear
amber|Performance|~filter early|WHERE shrinks input|HAVING runs on grouped data|prefer WHERE
rose|Rule|~by condition type|row value -> WHERE|aggregate value -> HAVING|

sections.title: WHERE + GROUP BY + HAVING together
sections.content:
```sql
SELECT department, COUNT(*) AS headcount
FROM employees
WHERE active = true          -- row filter first
GROUP BY department
HAVING COUNT(*) > 5          -- keep only big departments
ORDER BY headcount DESC;
```

Sample output:

| department | headcount |
|---|---|
| Tech | 12 |
| Sales | 7 |

*Active employees grouped by department, keeping only departments with more than five.*

sections.title: Wrong: an aggregate condition in WHERE
sections.content:
```sql
-- COUNT(*) does not exist yet when WHERE runs -> error
SELECT department, COUNT(*) AS headcount
FROM employees
WHERE COUNT(*) > 5
GROUP BY department;
```

sections.title: Right: the aggregate condition goes in HAVING
sections.content:
```sql
-- HAVING runs after grouping, so COUNT(*) is available
SELECT department, COUNT(*) AS headcount
FROM employees
GROUP BY department
HAVING COUNT(*) > 5;
```

*`WHERE` runs before groups exist, so it can't see `COUNT(*)`. Aggregate conditions only become legal once `GROUP BY` has formed the groups — that's `HAVING`'s job.*

sections.title: Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Aggregate in WHERE**: `WHERE COUNT(*) > 5` is illegal — use HAVING.
- **Row filter in HAVING**: works but is slower; put it in WHERE.
- **HAVING without GROUP BY**: legal in some DBs (treats whole table as one group), but usually a mistake.
- **Using a SELECT alias in HAVING**: portability varies — repeat the aggregate to be safe.

seo.metaTitle: HAVING Clause in SQL — Filtering Groups — java backend interview question | InterviewExplainer
seo.metaDescription: Interview answer for What is the HAVING clause in SQL and when do you use it? with a clear explanation, practical example, common mistakes, and follow-up questions.

speakable_v2.hook: HAVING is the only clause where a count or a sum can sit in a filter. It runs once the groups exist.
speakable_v2.standard_example: Departments kept by HAVING COUNT above five after GROUP BY

beats.text: HAVING filters the groups that GROUP BY makes. It checks aggregate values like count or sum for each group. So it's the group-level twin of WHERE, which filters rows.
WHERE can't test a count, because grouping hasn't happened when WHERE runs. The counts simply don't exist yet. HAVING fills that gap. It runs after the groups form, so it reads each group's total.

items: WHERE runs first and trims the rows going into the groups.
HAVING runs later and trims the groups coming back out.
Aggregate conditions like count greater than five only work here.

beats.text: Say you want busy departments. Filter active staff in WHERE, group by department, then keep groups with count above five in HAVING. Here's the non-obvious part. WHERE shrinks the input first, so HAVING only weighs the groups that survived.

items: Writing count greater than five in WHERE. That's illegal, since no groups exist yet.
Doing a plain row filter in HAVING. It works but it's slower than WHERE.

speakable_v2.cap: So HAVING filters groups after the math, and WHERE filters rows before it. Match the filter to the stage.

questions.question: How do you group by multiple columns in SQL?
questions.title: Grouping by Multiple Columns in SQL
questions.direct_answer: GROUP BY a, b creates one group for each distinct pair of a and b values. Reversing the grouping-expression order forms the same basic set of groups, though it does not define output order and can affect advanced grouping constructs or plans. Selected non-aggregate expressions must follow the database's grouping and functional-dependency rules.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you know multi-column GROUP BY groups by value combinations.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Expecting GROUP BY a, b to behave like grouping by a alone.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Note that all non-aggregated SELECT columns must appear in the multi-column GROUP BY.

sections.title: Grouping by a Combination of Columns
sections.content:
The common beginner rule says every selected non-aggregate column must appear in GROUP BY. SQL also permits functionally dependent expressions under defined rules, and database enforcement/extensions differ. For portable code, keep the relationship obvious.

Column order does not create hierarchical output by itself. GROUP BY region, product and GROUP BY product, region identify the same pairs in this simple query. ROLLUP and GROUPING SETS are different because expression ordering can define subtotal levels.

**Example.** GROUP BY region, status creates one group for each region/status pair, such as East/OPEN and East/CLOSED. SELECT region, status, COUNT(*) returns a count for every pair rather than separate independent totals.

sections.title: Quick revision
content: GROUP BY region, product -> one group per region/product pair.
Adding a grouping column usually makes groups more specific.
GROUP BY does not sort the result; add ORDER BY separately.
Do not select an arbitrary detail column that has several values within one group.

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content:
SELECT region, product, SUM(amount) FROM sale GROUP BY region, product returns totals for East/Phone, East/Cable, and each other combination. Grouping only by region combines all products in that region. NULL grouping values normally form a group under SQL grouping rules. Add ORDER BY region, product if display order matters.

For example, grouping orders by region and status produces one row for each pair, so East/OPEN and East/CLOSED are different groups with their own counts.

sections.title: Multi-Column GROUP BY at a Glance
sections.content:
blue|What|~groups by combination|one row per (a,b)|finer than single column|distinct pairs
emerald|Order|~doesn't change groups|GROUP BY a,b = b,a|same buckets|affects readability only
amber|SELECT rule|~all grouped cols allowed|every non-agg col in GROUP BY|aggregates summarize|
rose|Use|~cross-tab style|region x product|year x month|category breakdowns

sections.title: Group by two columns
sections.content:
```sql
SELECT region, product, SUM(amount) AS sales
FROM orders
GROUP BY region, product
ORDER BY region, sales DESC;
```

Sample output:

| region | product | sales |
|---|---|---|
| East | Phone | 9000 |
| East | Cable | 1200 |
| West | Phone | 7000 |

*One row per region-and-product combination.*

sections.title: Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Expecting single-column behaviour**: `GROUP BY region, product` splits each region into per-product rows.
- **Missing a SELECT column in GROUP BY**: every non-aggregated column must be listed.
- **Assuming column order matters**: it changes display logic, not the groups.
- **Too many GROUP BY columns**: over-splitting yields tiny, less useful groups.

seo.metaTitle: Grouping by Multiple Columns in SQL — java backend interview question | InterviewExplainer
seo.metaDescription: Interview answer for How do you group by multiple columns in SQL? with a clear explanation, practical example, common mistakes, and follow-up questions.

speakable_v2.hook: List two columns after GROUP BY and you don't group by the first one. You bucket every unique pair.
speakable_v2.standard_example: Sales grouped by region and product, one row per pair

beats.text: Grouping by several columns makes one group for each unique combination of their values. Group by region and product gives one row per region and product pair. That's finer than region alone.
One column gives a flat summary. Real reports need a grid. Sales by region and product, or signups by year and month. Multiple columns build that cross-tab breakdown in a single query.

items: Each distinct pair becomes its own bucket. East phones and East cables are two groups.
Column order doesn't change the groups. It only changes how rows sort and read.
Grouping by an expression works too, like the year of a hire date.

beats.text: Count hires per department per year. Group by department and the year of hire date, and each row is one department in one year. Here's the non-obvious part. Three teams across four years can make up to twelve groups, not three.

items: Expecting it to act like one column. Each region now splits into per-product rows.
Adding too many columns. You end up with tiny groups that don't tell you much.

speakable_v2.cap: So extra GROUP BY columns mean finer buckets, one row for each unique combination you list.

questions.question: What is the SQL execution order for GROUP BY queries?
questions.title: SQL Execution Order with GROUP BY and HAVING
questions.direct_answer: A useful logical order is FROM/JOIN -> WHERE -> GROUP BY -> HAVING -> SELECT -> DISTINCT -> ORDER BY -> row limiting. This explains why WHERE filters input rows and HAVING filters groups. It is a semantic model, not the database's physical execution schedule; optimizers reorder operations while preserving results. Alias visibility and LIMIT/FETCH syntax vary in some database extensions.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you know where GROUP BY/HAVING sit in execution order.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Thinking HAVING runs before grouping or that SELECT aliases work in WHERE.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Tie the order to why aggregates need HAVING and aliases fail in WHERE.

sections.title: Logical Processing Order for a Grouped Query
sections.content:
A database need not physically scan, group, then filter in exactly that sequence. It can push predicates, use indexes, or combine operators. The logical order exists to define the result.

SELECT aliases are normally unavailable in WHERE under standard SQL, but some engines expose aliases in additional clauses. Teach the standard rule and verify dialect extensions. Do not infer that an earlier logical clause is always physically faster.

sections.title: Quick revision
content: FROM/JOIN builds the input relation.
WHERE removes rows before grouping.
GROUP BY forms groups; HAVING removes groups.
SELECT forms output; ORDER BY orders it; LIMIT/OFFSET/FETCH restricts rows using vendor syntax.

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content: In SELECT department, COUNT(*) AS headcount FROM employee WHERE active=true GROUP BY department HAVING COUNT(*)>5 ORDER BY headcount DESC, active rows are the grouped input, the count condition is evaluated per group, and the alias is available to ORDER BY in standard/common behavior. WHERE cannot use COUNT(*) because group values do not yet exist in the logical model.

sections.title: Grouped Query Flow
sections.content:
```mermaid flowchart TB A[FROM
read table] --> B[WHERE
filter rows] B --> C[GROUP BY
form groups] C --> D[HAVING
filter groups w/ aggregates] D --> E[SELECT
compute columns + aliases] E --> F[ORDER BY
sort, aliases OK] F --> G[LIMIT
cap rows] ```

sections.title: Each clause in its place
sections.content:
```sql
SELECT department, COUNT(*) AS headcount   -- 5: compute output
FROM employees                              -- 1: read
WHERE active = true                         -- 2: filter rows
GROUP BY department                         -- 3: form groups
HAVING COUNT(*) > 5                          -- 4: filter groups
ORDER BY headcount DESC                      -- 6: sort (alias OK)
LIMIT 10;                                    -- 7: cap
```

Sample output:

| department | headcount |
|---|---|
| Tech | 12 |
| Sales | 7 |

sections.title: Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **HAVING before grouping**: HAVING runs *after* GROUP BY — it needs the groups to exist.
- **Alias in WHERE**: WHERE runs before SELECT computes the alias.
- **Aggregate in WHERE**: no groups yet — use HAVING.
- **Filtering rows in HAVING**: slower; do row filters in WHERE.

seo.metaDescription: Interview answer for What is the SQL execution order for GROUP BY queries? with a clear explanation, practical example, common mistakes, and follow-up questions.

speakable_v2.hook: SQL's logical processing order explains grouped-query semantics; the optimizer can choose a different physical execution plan.
speakable_v2.standard_example: FROM, WHERE, GROUP BY, HAVING, SELECT, ORDER BY, LIMIT in order

beats.text: A grouped query always runs in one logical order. It's not the order you type the clauses in. The engine reads and filters the rows, groups them, then shapes the result.
This single order answers the tricky questions. Why must aggregates live in HAVING? Why do aliases fail in WHERE? Both come straight from when each clause runs.

steps: HAVING filters those buckets with aggregates.
SELECT builds the columns and aliases.

beats.text: Take count of staff per active department. WHERE keeps active rows. GROUP BY buckets them. HAVING keeps the big ones and ORDER BY sorts. Here's the non-obvious part. ORDER BY can use a SELECT alias because it runs after SELECT, while WHERE can't.

items: Thinking HAVING runs before grouping. It needs the groups to already exist.
Using a SELECT alias in WHERE. The alias isn't built until SELECT runs.

speakable_v2.cap: So that order, FROM through LIMIT, explains why aggregates need HAVING and aliases die in WHERE.

questions.question: What is the difference between WHERE and HAVING in terms of performance?
questions.title: WHERE vs HAVING Performance in SQL
questions.direct_answer: WHERE filters rows before grouping; HAVING filters groups after aggregation. Put a condition in WHERE when it is a row-level rule and in HAVING when it depends on an aggregate or group. This often reduces work, but saying WHERE is always faster is too strong: optimizers can push equivalent predicates, indexes and plans differ, and some conditions are not semantically movable.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you understand the performance reason to filter in WHERE before grouping.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Doing row-level filtering in HAVING, making the database group rows it will throw away.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Say: filter early, aggregate late — only aggregate conditions justify HAVING.

sections.title: WHERE and HAVING: Semantics Before Speed
sections.content:
The important boundary is semantics. Moving HAVING COUNT(*) > 3 to WHERE is impossible because no per-row count exists yet. Moving a grouping-key predicate may be valid. Moving a predicate on a nullable side of an outer join can change which groups survive.

Start with the correct result, then inspect the plan and row estimates. Avoid teaching clause order as a stopwatch where every earlier clause is automatically faster.

**Example.** To count paid orders by customer, WHERE status='PAID' removes unpaid rows before GROUP BY. Putting an equivalent non-aggregate condition in HAVING may be rejected or transformed by the optimizer, but WHERE states the intent clearly and can reduce input early.

sections.title: Quick revision
content: Row condition such as status = 'PAID' belongs in WHERE.
Group condition such as COUNT(*) >= 5 belongs in HAVING.
Moving a condition can change the answer, not merely performance.
Use EXPLAIN/EXPLAIN ANALYZE to compare real plans.

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content:
WHERE amount > 0 removes rows before SUM(amount) is computed. HAVING SUM(amount) > 1000 must wait until each group total exists. HAVING status = 'PAID' can be logically equivalent to a WHERE predicate in some grouped queries and a database may push it down, but writing the row filter in WHERE makes intent clear. Performance follows the optimized plan, not only the logical clause order.

For example, WHERE order_date >= DATE '2026-01-01' filters rows before grouping, while HAVING COUNT(*) >= 10 keeps only completed groups with ten or more rows.

sections.title: WHERE vs HAVING Performance
sections.content:
emerald|WHERE|~filter early|runs before GROUP BY|fewer rows to group|index-friendly
rose|HAVING|~filter late|runs after GROUP BY|groups then discards|wasted work for row filters
blue|Principle|~filter early aggregate late|push row filters to WHERE|HAVING only for aggregates|
amber|Result|~same answer|but different cost|WHERE usually cheaper|measure with EXPLAIN

sections.title: Performance Comparison
sections.content:
| Aspect | WHERE | HAVING |
|---|---|---|
| Runs | before GROUP BY | after GROUP BY |
| Rows grouped | fewer (filtered) | all, then discarded |
| Index use | possible | not on the filter |
| Best for | row conditions | aggregate conditions |

sections.title: Slow: row filter done in HAVING
sections.content:
```sql
-- groups EVERY department, then drops 'CONTRACT' ones
SELECT department, COUNT(*) AS c
FROM employees
GROUP BY department
HAVING department <> 'CONTRACT';   -- row condition in the wrong place
```

sections.title: Fast: row filter in WHERE
sections.content:
```sql
-- excludes rows BEFORE grouping -> fewer rows to group
SELECT department, COUNT(*) AS c
FROM employees
WHERE department <> 'CONTRACT'      -- filter early
GROUP BY department;
```

*Same result, but the WHERE version groups fewer rows and can use an index on `department`.*

sections.title: When to Use Which
sections.content:
Use **WHERE** for any condition on a raw column (status, date, id) — it filters before grouping and can use indexes.

Use **HAVING** only when the filter depends on an aggregate (`COUNT(*) > 5`, `SUM(total) > 10000`). If a condition can be expressed without an aggregate, it belongs in WHERE.

seo.metaTitle: WHERE vs HAVING Performance in SQL — java backend interview question | InterviewExplainer
seo.metaDescription: Interview answer for What is the difference between WHERE and HAVING in terms of performance? with a clear explanation, practical example, common mistakes, and follow-up questions.

speakable_v2.hook: Put a row filter in HAVING and the database groups everything first, then throws half of it away.
speakable_v2.standard_example: A row filter pushed into WHERE before GROUP BY

beats.text: WHERE and HAVING both filter, but they don't run at the same stage. WHERE runs before grouping and cuts raw rows. HAVING runs after grouping and cuts whole groups by their aggregates.
Reach for WHERE whenever you're testing a plain column, like a status or a date. Save HAVING for aggregate tests, like count above five. If it isn't an aggregate, it doesn't belong in HAVING.
Say a million rows shrink to ten thousand active ones. In WHERE, only those ten thousand get grouped. Important: the same test in HAVING groups all million first.

speakable_v2.cap: So filter early in WHERE and keep HAVING for real aggregate tests. Same answer, much less work.
followup_handoff: Is there any case where a non-aggregate condition belongs in HAVING?

questions.question: Write a SQL query to find departments with more than 3 employees earning above 50000.
questions.title: SQL Query — WHERE + GROUP BY + HAVING Combined
questions.direct_answer: Filter employees with salary > 50000 in WHERE, group the remaining rows by department, and keep groups whose COUNT(*) is greater than 3 in HAVING. The query answers 'departments with more than three employees who each earn above 50000.' Include the department key/name consistently and add ORDER BY only when a result order is required.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you can correctly place a row filter in WHERE and a count filter in HAVING.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Putting the salary filter in HAVING or the COUNT condition in WHERE.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Explain why salary>50000 must be in WHERE (per-row) and COUNT>3 in HAVING (per-group).

sections.title: Combining WHERE, GROUP BY, and HAVING
sections.content:
If the result needs department_name from a department table, join it and group according to the database's grouping/functional-dependency rules. Grouping by a stable department id avoids merging two departments that share a display name.

Parameterize the salary threshold in application code. The query is about correct placement, not a universal performance claim that WHERE is always faster than HAVING.

sections.title: Quick revision
content: WHERE salary > 50000 is a row condition.
GROUP BY department forms one group per department.
HAVING COUNT(*) > 3 is a group condition.
COUNT(*) counts only rows that survived WHERE.

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content:
~~~sql
SELECT department_id, COUNT(*) AS high_earners
FROM employee
WHERE salary > 50000
GROUP BY department_id
HAVING COUNT(*) > 3
ORDER BY high_earners DESC, department_id;
~~~

A department with ten employees but only three above 50000 is excluded because the WHERE clause removes the other seven before counting. Greater than three means at least four; use >= 3 only if the requirement changes to three or more.

For example, WHERE status='PAID' keeps paid orders, GROUP BY customer_id forms each customer's group, and HAVING SUM(total) > 1000 keeps customers whose paid total exceeds 1000.

sections.title: Query Plan at a Glance
sections.content:
emerald|WHERE|~per-row filter|salary > 50000|keep high earners|runs before grouping
blue|GROUP BY|~bucket rows|by department|one group each|enables COUNT
amber|HAVING|~per-group filter|COUNT(*) > 3|keep big groups|runs after grouping
rose|Trap|~swap them|salary in HAVING = wrong|COUNT in WHERE = error|placement matters

sections.title: The complete query
sections.content:
```sql
SELECT department, COUNT(*) AS high_earners
FROM employees
WHERE salary > 50000        -- per-row: only high earners enter the groups
GROUP BY department
HAVING COUNT(*) > 3         -- per-group: keep departments with > 3 of them
ORDER BY high_earners DESC;
```

Sample output:

| department | high_earners |
|---|---|
| Engineering | 7 |
| Sales | 4 |

*Only departments where more than three employees earn above 50000.*

sections.title: Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Salary filter in HAVING**: `HAVING salary > 50000` is wrong — salary is per-row, not an aggregate.
- **COUNT in WHERE**: `WHERE COUNT(*) > 3` is illegal — no groups exist yet.
- **Counting everyone**: forgetting the WHERE means you count all employees, not just high earners.
- **No ORDER BY**: output order is undefined without it.

speakable_v2.hook: This classic asks for two filters, and each one has a different home in the query.
speakable_v2.standard_example: Departments with more than three employees earning above fifty thousand

beats.text: The task hides two filters of different kinds. Earning above fifty thousand is a per-row test. More than three employees is a per-group count. Each belongs in its own clause.
Placement's the whole point. A row test runs before grouping, so it goes in WHERE. A count only exists after grouping, so it goes in HAVING. Mix them up and the query breaks or lies.

items: WHERE salary above fifty thousand keeps only the high earners.
GROUP BY department buckets those earners by team.
HAVING count above three keeps teams with enough of them.

beats.text: Run it on an employees table. WHERE trims to high earners, GROUP BY splits them by department, HAVING keeps departments with more than three. Here's the non-obvious part. Because WHERE runs first, the count's a count of high earners only, not everyone.

items: Putting salary in HAVING. Salary isn't an aggregate, so that test belongs in WHERE.
Putting the count in WHERE. No groups exist yet, so the query errors out.

speakable_v2.cap: So send the row test to WHERE and the count test to HAVING, and the query writes itself.
